extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of classical literature and ancient drama
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the characteristic features, compositional practices, and evaluative attributes of Plautus's comedies as described in the Wikipedia article. Useful for anyone studying Roman comedy, humor techniques, or adaptation from Greek New Comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation from Greek New Comedy / Romanization
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautus's comedies are mostly adapted from Greek models and often based directly on the works of the Greek playwrights; he reworked the Greek texts to give them a flavour that would appeal to the local Roman audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a play preserves the Greek plot structure while inserting Roman cultural references, local humour, and modifications in characterization; successful Plautine adaptation balances fidelity to source plots with changes that make the material resonate for Roman audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prologues: verbosity to win the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'verbosity of the Plautine prologues has often been commented upon and generally excused by the necessity of the Roman playwright to win his audience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate prologues for their audience-orienting function: length and directness can be justified if they successfully prepare or entice the audience; judge prologues by their effectiveness in setting up plot/context rather than strict brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wordplay, puns and paronomasia
rubrics_metrics.description: Word play is essential to Plautine comedy: Plautus is well known for his devotion to puns, alliteration and paronomasia (punning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider density and inventiveness of verbal wit (puns, name-play, alliteration) as a core comic resource; names and diction that create double meanings are hallmarks of Plautine humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal comedy over physical comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautus often makes up for lack of physical comedy with words, relying more on wordplay and verbal devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating comic effect, weigh the strength of verbal techniques (dialogue, rhetorical devices, jokes) rather than expecting primarily slapstick or physical stage business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stock characters (slaves, concubines, soldiers, old men)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautus works with stock characters inherited from Greek comedy—roles such as slaves, concubines, soldiers, and old men—while injecting his own innovations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess characterization by how effectively stock types are used or innovated upon; originality often lies in Plautus' modifications of familiar archetypes rather than wholly new character types.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'clever slave' archetype
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plautine 'clever slave' provides exposition and humor and often drives the plot; Plautus altered the stock slave character to create a stronger, plot-driving figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the slave-figure's role in plot propulsion, comic invention, and social commentary; a successful Plautine slave both produces comic set-pieces and manipulates events to resolve the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Farce and reduced believability
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautus' plays are often more farcical and less believable than Menander's; this 'incredulity' is a feature of Plautine comedy rather than a flaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Plautine plays on their intended farcical terms—heightened improbability, broad situations, and exaggerated characters are acceptable and often desirable comic techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic focus: father–son and household relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: A main theme inherited from New Comedy is the father–son relationship and emphasis on household/domestic situations (situations that develop in the bosom of the family).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing plots and moral stakes, give attention to household dynamics, filial piety, and domestic duty as central motives and sources of conflict and resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of recognition tokens and reunion devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautine plots commonly use recognition tokens (e.g., a little casket of tokens) and last-act recognitions to resolve identity and reunion plots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate plot mechanics for how convincingly and theatrically recognition tokens are employed to bring about denouement; such devices are conventional and expected in Plautine structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical allusions and audience engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautus sometimes inserts highly specific allusions (e.g., references to the Second Punic War) intended to be comprehensible to and rile up contemporary audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the presence and effectiveness of topical references in engaging the audience and shaping interpretive context; topicality is a tool for immediacy and rhetorical impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreverence toward the gods as comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautus was sometimes accused of teaching the public indifference and mockery of the gods by comparing mortals with gods or scornfully referencing deities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the degree of irreverence as deliberate comic shading—judge whether comparisons/insults to the gods function as satire, social commentary, or mere comic exaggeration, keeping in mind historical limits on risqué material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing risqué material with censorship risks
rubrics_metrics.description: The state controlled stage productions and Plautus' plays would have been banned had they been too risqué.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether sexual or irreverent content is calibrated to entertain without crossing contemporary legal/social prohibitions; skillful Plautine comedy pushes boundaries while avoiding outright prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive modification of characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautus could substantially modify characterization and thus change the emphasis of a play; he injected creativity into stock roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess originality by looking for substantive changes to stock types (motivation, agency, comic strategies) that alter the play's tone or thematic focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prologue and metatheatrical commentary as orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prologues often introduce the play, explain circumstances, and guide audience expectations; they are a significant structural and rhetorical element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how prologues frame reception (moralizing, apologetic, teasing) and whether they effectively prepare the audience for the play's conventions and comic stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on linguistic archaisms and diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautus's diction incorporates archaic forms and specific word-studies (verb forms, nouns) which shape its poetic register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess linguistic texture (archaisms, colloquialisms, register shifts) for their contribution to comic voice and historical color, taking into account possible transmission and manuscript variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of music, rhythm and 'numeri' in performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautine plays include musical elements and metrical numbers ('numeri innumeri'), contributing to their comic and performative effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging performative qualities, attend to meter, rhythm, and song as integral to comedic timing and audience pleasure; music can amplify jokes and character moods.
